newsitem.title: USA: Six US lawmakers file suit to stop line-item veto.
newsitem.headline: Six US lawmakers file suit to stop line-item veto.

text.p: Six members of Congress filed suit in federal court on Thursday seeking to overturn a new law that allows the president to veto individual tax and spending items contained in larger bills passed by Congress.

Lawmakers filing the suit included West Virginia Democratic Sen. Robert Byrd and New York Democratic Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan. The sole Republican to join in filing the suit was retiring Oregon Republican Sen. Mark Hatfield.
The lawmakers asked the court to move fast to overturn the line-item veto law, which they argued violates the U.S. Constitution.

The line-item veto or "enhanced rescissions" law, was passed by Congress last year and took effect Jan. 1. For the first time, it allows the president to sign a bill into law while canceling individual spending, tax or appropriations items embedded in the broader legislation.

In the past, the president had to sign or veto legislation in its entirety. This allowed members of Congress to pad major legislation with unrelated spending or tax measures for individual districts or interest groups that may not have passed on their own.
Under the new law, it would take a two-thirds vote of Congress to override a line-item veto, just as with a regular veto.

The line-item veto's opponents argue that the law violates Article I of the Constitution, which reqiures that a bill be passed by a majority vote in both houses of Congress and be approved or vetoed in its entirety by the president.

"The act unconstitutionally expands the president's power," the lawmakers argue in their lawsuit, adding that "the act grants powers to the president that contravene the constitutional process for making federal law."

The line-item veto was a key part of House Republicans' Contract with America. Lawmakers committed to cutting federal spending had argued in favor of the law for years, calling it a needed tool to reduce wasteful federal spending.
Opponents of the law warned that Congress would rue the day it voted to transfer some of its budgetary powers to the executive branch of government.

The lawsuit charges that the new law altered the legal and practical effect of all votes that lawmakers cast on bills subject to the line-item veto; divested Congress of its constitutional role in repealing legislation and altered the constitutional balance of power between the legislative and executive branches.
Sponsors of the new law expected a court challenge, so the new law includes a special procedure to speed review by the U.S. Supreme Court, which has the final say on disputes over the Constitution.
